notice: ALL PAPERS, PEOPLE, RESULTS AND SOURCES BELOW ARE FICTIONAL ENGINEERING DATA, NOT REAL RESEARCH.
question: How do retrieval-task designs and learner contexts relate to retention and participation in the fictional instructional corpus?

papers.title: FICTIONAL A retrieval logs
papers.context: Synthetic urban adult evening classes; voluntary practice
papers.limitations: Selection and prior knowledge uncontrolled; no causal identification; immediate and delayed measures differ

evidence.source_text: FICTIONAL A: Voluntary retrieval frequency was positively associated with immediate factual-test scores. Selection and prior knowledge were uncontrolled.
FICTIONAL A: The association with delayed conceptual-transfer scores was null in the measured class; this was not an equivalence test.

papers.title: FICTIONAL B timed recall comparison
papers.context: Synthetic rural adult classes; imposed timed retrieval
papers.limitations: Single synthetic classroom allocation; no inference beyond context; different outcome and delivery from A

evidence.source_text: FICTIONAL B: Classes assigned timed retrieval had lower immediate free-recall scores than classes assigned restudy. This pattern conflicts with an unconditional benefit proposition, not with A's local observation.

papers.title: FICTIONAL C learner accounts
papers.context: Synthetic adult evening-course accounts of voluntary and timed practice
papers.limitations: Analyst-created fictional themes; no participant quotations; experiences do not estimate effects

evidence.source_text: FICTIONAL C: Interpretive analysis associated voluntary practice with perceived autonomy, while timed tasks were described as pressure. These are analytic interpretations, not measured retention effects.
FICTIONAL C: Accounts of participation were mixed, including engagement and withdrawal; neither theme was universal.

papers.title: FICTIONAL D feedback proposition
papers.context: Synthetic conceptual model of retrieval and feedback
papers.limitations: No original empirical mechanism test; original secondary source not inspected

evidence.source_text: FICTIONAL D: Feedback timing is proposed as a mechanism that could alter retrieval-task usefulness. The proposition has not been empirically tested in this source.
FICTIONAL D: An uninspected prior report is cited as suggesting a feedback advantage. This secondary statement does not independently verify that prior result.
evidence.secondary_source_reference: FICTIONAL uninspected prior report; deliberately no fabricated DOI

evidence.source_text: FICTIONAL D: Whether feedback explains the differing patterns in A and B is unresolved; no mediation estimate or comparative test is available.
